title: Number of Subarrays with Bounded Maximum
description: Brute force to optimized: tracking a running maximum per subarray versus the atMost(right) - atMost(left-1) reduction using run-length counting.

content.title: Number of Subarrays with Bounded Maximum

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and two integers left and right, return the number of contiguous, non-empty subarrays whose maximum element falls within the inclusive range [left, right].

blocks.caption: Count subarrays with max <= right, minus those with max <= left - 1, to isolate the range

blocks.text: Given nums, left, and right, count how many contiguous, non-empty subarrays have their maximum element somewhere within the inclusive range [left, right].

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Stretches of a Fence Within a Height Range
blocks.text: Like inspecting a long fence made of vertical slats of varying heights and counting every contiguous stretch whose TALLEST slat falls within an allowed height range. It's easier to first count every stretch whose tallest slat is at most the range's upper bound, then separately count every stretch whose tallest slat is at most JUST BELOW the range's lower bound, and subtract: what remains is exactly the stretches whose tallest slat falls inside the desired range.

blocks.caption: Every new qualifying element extends the run, contributing exactly its run length in new valid subarrays

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Subarrays with max <= 3: [2], [2,1], [3] -> 4 total (using the run-length counting trick, not enumeration)","countAtMost(3) = 4","Every subarray whose maximum is at most 3"],["Subarrays with max <= 1 (left - 1 = 1): [1] -> 1 total","countAtMost(1) = 1","Only the single-element subarray [1] has its maximum at most 1"],["Answer","3","4 - 1 = 3: the qualifying subarrays are [2], [2,1], and [3], each with max in [2,3]"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Subarrays with max <= 8: several short stretches, excluding any subarray touching the 9","countAtMost(8) computed via run-length tracking","The 9 breaks any potential run immediately"],["Subarrays with max <= 1 (left - 1 = 1): none, since every element is at least 2","countAtMost(1) = 0","No element in nums is small enough to ever qualify"],["Answer","7","countAtMost(8) - countAtMost(1) = 7 - 0 = 7"]]}

blocks.text: Before checking every subarray's maximum directly, notice that counting "max <= bound" subarrays can be done very efficiently by tracking runs, and that the target range reduces to two such counts subtracted.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: "Maximum falls in [left, right]" is exactly "(maximum <= right)" minus "(maximum <= left - 1)", the same atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) reduction used for exact-sum counting problems, applied here to a maximum-value condition instead of a sum condition.

Observation 2: Counting "subarrays with max <= bound" doesn't require tracking an actual running maximum per subarray. Instead, track the length of the current unbroken RUN of consecutive elements that are all <= bound.

Observation 3: Every time the run extends by one more qualifying element, exactly (current run length) NEW valid subarrays are created: one ending here of length 1, one of length 2, and so on, up to the full run length, since every subarray fully contained within the current run automatically has max <= bound.

Observation 4: The moment an element exceeds bound, no subarray can span across it, so the run resets completely to 0.

Recognizing that counting "at most" subarrays reduces to simple run-length bookkeeping (rather than tracking an actual running maximum) is what makes both required counts computable in a single linear pass each.
This is the atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) reduction (as seen in Binary Subarrays with Sum), paired with a run-length counting technique specifically suited to "maximum stays within a bound" conditions.
For every possible starting index, extend forward, tracking the running maximum directly, and check whether it falls within [left, right] at every step.

items: For every possible starting index, walk forward, updating a running maximum as each new element is included.
At every step, check whether the running maximum falls within [left, right], incrementing the count if so.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A fresh running maximum is used for every starting position, since each independent walk tracks its own subarray's maximum.
The running maximum only ever increases as the subarray grows (never decreases), since max() only ever keeps the larger value.
count increments at every step where the current running maximum satisfies the range condition, regardless of prior steps.

blocks.text: Every possible subarray's maximum is checked directly, so the correct count is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since each of the n starting positions walks forward up to n elements.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: tracking an actual running maximum for every starting position ignores that "max <= bound" subarrays can be counted directly and far more cheaply using simple run-length bookkeeping, without ever needing to know the exact maximum value of any subarray.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force tracks an actual running maximum for every starting position. Instead, define countAtMost(bound), which counts subarrays with max <= bound using only a running RUN LENGTH: increment the run whenever the current element is <= bound (adding the run length to the total, since every subarray ending here within the run qualifies), and reset the run to 0 the moment an element exceeds bound. The final answer is countAtMost(right) - countAtMost(left - 1).

Implement countAtMost(bound) as a single pass: maintain run, incrementing it when the current element is <= bound and adding it to a running total each time, or resetting it to 0 when the current element exceeds bound. The final answer is countAtMost(right) minus countAtMost(left - 1).
Compute countAtMost(right) and countAtMost(left - 1) using run-length tracking, then subtract.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: countAtMost(3) - countAtMost(1) = 4 - 1 = 3, matching the expected answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), since countAtMost runs a single linear pass, and it's called exactly twice.
Space: O(1) extra.

Within any unbroken run of consecutive elements all <= bound, EVERY contiguous sub-stretch of that run automatically has max <= bound too, since every element in it individually satisfies the bound. A run of length L ending at the current position contributes exactly L new valid subarrays ending here (of lengths 1 through L), which is exactly what adding the current run length to the total captures. The moment an element exceeds bound, no subarray can span across it, so the run must reset completely.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Current element <= bound","Extend the run by 1, and add the new run length to the running total"],["Current element > bound","Reset the run to 0; no subarray ending here can have max <= bound"]]}

items: countAtMost is a single reusable helper, called with two different bound values (right, then left - 1).
run tracks only a LENGTH, never an actual maximum value, since the bound comparison alone is sufficient to determine validity.
total accumulates the run length at every qualifying step, correctly counting every new subarray introduced by extending the run by one more position.

blocks.text: The atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) reduction generalizes beyond exact-sum problems (as in Binary Subarrays with Sum) to any "value falls in a range" counting problem, and "max <= bound" specifically reduces to simple run-length bookkeeping rather than tracking an actual maximum.

items: Tracking an actual running maximum value instead of just a run LENGTH, which works but is an unnecessary complication once the run-length trick is recognized.
Forgetting that countAtMost(left - 1), not countAtMost(left), is the correct second term, since the range [left, right] is inclusive on both ends.
Miscounting the contribution of a run: it's the run length ADDED to the total at each step (representing every new subarray ending at the current position), not just 1 added per qualifying element.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["left = 0","left - 1 = -1, and countAtMost(-1) is naturally 0, since no element can ever be <= -1 (assuming non-negative array values)"],["Every element in nums falls within [left, right]","The answer equals the total number of possible non-empty subarrays, n*(n+1)/2"],["No element in nums falls within [left, right]","The answer is 0"]]}

items: Explicitly state the atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) reduction and connect it to Binary Subarrays with Sum's identical technique, since recognizing this reusable reduction (applied to a different underlying condition) demonstrates strong pattern transfer.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Count subarrays whose maximum (or minimum, or any monotonic property) falls within a RANGE" points toward the atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) reduction, with the "at most" count computed via whatever technique (run-length tracking, sliding window, etc.) fits that specific condition.

items: How would you count subarrays whose MINIMUM (not maximum) falls in a range? The same atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) structure applies, but "at most" would need to become "at least" (or the bound direction flipped), requiring a mirrored run-length technique.

How would you find the actual longest or shortest such subarray, not just the count? A different tracking approach (recording start/end indices of runs) would be needed instead of just accumulating a count.

Could this be solved with a monotonic stack instead? Yes, a monotonic stack can also count subarrays by maximum value in various ways, though the run-length technique here is simpler for this specific "count all such subarrays" formulation.

The atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) reduction, shared with Binary Subarrays with Sum, applied here to a maximum-value bound instead of a sum, combined with a run-length counting technique specific to "all elements below a bound" conditions.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (atMost(right) - atMost(left-1)): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) exact-range reduction, using run-length counting for each "at most" pass
Core Idea: Counting subarrays with max in [left, right] equals counting those with max <= right, minus those with max <= left - 1
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: "Max <= bound" subarrays can be counted via simple run-length bookkeeping, since every sub-stretch of a qualifying run automatically qualifies too
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: countAtMost(right) - countAtMost(left - 1), where countAtMost tracks a run length
